newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian ski resort landslide buries up to 20.
newsitem.headline: Australian ski resort landslide buries up to 20.

text.p: As dawn broke over Australia's most popular ski resort Thredbo on Thursday it revealed the splintered remains of two ski lodges which collapsed under a landslide, possibly burying up to 20 people.
"It looks very dismal," said police chief superintendent Charlie Sanderson, when asked whether there were any survivors.
Light snow dusted a handful of rescue workers as they cautiously inspected the twisted ruins of the lodges, which police said were too dangerously unstable for a rescue bid.
An eyewitness said the scene looked like the aftermath of a tornado, with debris scattered over the mountain side.

Television footage of the site revealed the landslide gouged a huge chunk out of the side of the mountain, dumping tonnes of dirt, rock and gum trees onto the first lodge Carinya and sending it cascading onto the second, Bimbadeen.
Police said they believe up to 20 people were in the lodges.
Several hundred metres of the mountain side, on which the Thredbo Alpine Village is perched, were littered with debris. Wrecked cars protruded from beneath the rubble.

"The Carinya lodge, which was on the upper side of the hill...that has virtually exploded as it has been hit and then it's cascaded down over the road and pancaked on top of a smaller lodge called the Bimbadeen," Glenn Milne, who was staying in a neighbouring lodge, told Channel Seven television.
"We just heard this enormous rush like I'd imagine you'd experience with a tornado just hitting a building...," said Milne, a television reporter.
Immediately after the landslide, anti-theft alarms from buried cars sent out calls for help from beneath the rubble.
Lodges further down the slope escaped the landslide, allowing rescuers easy road access to the scene and for evacuations.

The landslide occured just before midnight on Wednesday at a time when Thredbo, in the Snowy Mountains about 150 km (90 miles) southwest of Canberra, is packed with thousands of Australian and foreigners at the height of the local ski season.
Milne said residents in nearby lodges rushed to the collapsed buildings and began frantically digging in the rubble trying to reach survivors in the freezing, dark night.
"We got down into the rubble and we started clawing away chunks of rubble," Milne said.
"When the lodges collapsed, cars also came down on top -- they were teetering on the edge of the rubble. Every time we moved chunks of rubble, the cars were unstable at the top."
Milne said he heard three voices when he first reached the scene, but by daybreak silence enveloped the remains of the lodges.
